title: When would you choose AWS Lambda over a container (ECS/EKS), and what are Lambda's constraints (cold starts, max execution time, memory/CPU coupling, statelessness)?
shortTitle: When to Choose Lambda Over a Container, and Lambda's Constraints

s1_definition.profdef: You choose AWS Lambda over a container when the workload is short-lived, event-driven, spiky or infrequent, and benefits from scaling to zero with no server management, because Lambda runs code only on invocation and bills per millisecond. You keep a container on ECS or EKS when the workload is long-running, steady, latency-sensitive in a way cold starts would harm, needs more than Lambda's limits, or requires full runtime control. Lambda's main constraints are cold starts (added latency when a new execution environment initializes), a maximum execution time of fifteen minutes, memory and CPU that are coupled so you buy CPU by raising memory, and statelessness, meaning no reliable local state persists between invocations.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of two ways to staff a desk at National Bank of India. A container is a clerk who sits at the desk all day, every day, ready instantly — great if customers come constantly, but you pay the clerk even when no one shows up. Lambda is an on-call clerk who only walks in when a specific form arrives, handles it, and leaves — you pay only for those minutes, but there is a short wait while the clerk walks in from home (the cold start), the clerk must finish within a strict time limit, the clerk cannot keep personal notes between visits (statelessness), and to give the clerk a faster brain you also have to give them a bigger desk (memory and CPU are tied together).
s1_definition.oneliner: Choose Lambda for short, event-driven, spiky work that scales to zero, but respect its cold starts, fifteen-minute limit, memory-coupled CPU, and statelessness; keep containers for long-running, steady, or heavy workloads.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You choose AWS Lambda over a container when the workload is short-lived, event-driven, spiky or infrequent, and benefits from scaling to zero with no server management, because Lambda runs code only on invocation and bills per millisecond. You keep a container on ECS or EKS when the workload is long-running, steady, latency-sensitive in a way cold starts would harm, needs more than Lambda's limits, or requires full runtime control. Lambda's main constraints are cold starts (added latency when a new execution environment initializes), a maximum execution time of fifteen minutes, memory and CPU that are coupled so you buy CPU by raising memory, and statelessness, meaning no reliable local state persists between invocations.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of two ways to staff a desk at National Bank of India. A container is a clerk who sits at the desk all day, every day, ready instantly — great if customers come constantly, but you pay the clerk even when no one shows up. Lambda is an on-call clerk who only walks in when a specific form arrives, handles it, and leaves — you pay only for those minutes, but there is a short wait while the clerk walks in from home (the cold start), the clerk must finish within a strict time limit, the clerk cannot keep personal notes between visits (statelessness), and to give the clerk a faster brain you also have to give them a bigger desk (memory and CPU are tied together).

**One line to remember:** Choose Lambda for short, event-driven, spiky work that scales to zero, but respect its cold starts, fifteen-minute limit, memory-coupled CPU, and statelessness; keep containers for long-running, steady, or heavy workloads.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has two jobs. One reacts to a statement PDF landing in S3 and must index it — it runs a few hundred times a day in bursts. The other is the always-on transfer API handling steady traffic all day. Running the bursty job as an always-on container wastes money, and running the steady API as a function would pay cold-start latency constantly. This is exactly what choosing Lambda versus a container per workload solves.

Problem 2 — A nightly reconciliation job runs for forty minutes. Lambda's fifteen-minute limit forbids it as a single function. This is exactly why that job must be a container or be split into Step Functions steps.

We will write a small decision-and-simulation tool. `LambdaFunction` models cold-start latency, a max-duration limit, and statelessness. `WorkloadPlacement` decides Lambda versus container for a workload and flags when a job exceeds the fifteen-minute limit. The demo evaluates the bursty indexer, the steady API, and the long reconciliation job.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three jobs — a statement indexer (event-driven, thirty seconds, bursty), a transfer API (steady, always-on), and a nightly reconciliation (forty minutes). Then a cold-versus-warm invocation of the indexer function.

Step 1. The statement indexer is evaluated. Its duration of thirty seconds is well under the fifteen-minute limit, and it is event-driven and not steady, so the planner recommends Lambda. It will run only when a PDF lands and cost nothing in between.

Step 2. The transfer API is evaluated. It is steady, always-on traffic, so the planner recommends a container, because running it as a function would pay cold-start latency on scale-out constantly and a steady process is cheaper on a container.

Step 3. The nightly reconciliation is evaluated. Its duration of forty minutes exceeds the fifteen-minute Lambda limit, so the planner immediately recommends a container or splitting it into Step Functions steps. The time limit alone decides it.

Step 4. The indexer function is invoked cold. Because a fresh execution environment must download code and start the runtime, the latency is eight hundred milliseconds. This is the cold-start cost paid on the first invocation or during scale-out.

Step 5. The indexer function is invoked warm. The execution environment is reused, so initialization is skipped and the latency drops to fifteen milliseconds. This shows why keeping functions warm or using provisioned concurrency matters for latency-sensitive paths.

Step 6. The final output logs the three placements and the cold-versus-warm latencies.

```
2026-10-29 02:40:00 [INFO] statement-indexer -> LAMBDA (event-driven, short, scales to zero, pay-per-ms)
2026-10-29 02:40:00 [INFO] transfer-api -> CONTAINER (steady traffic; avoid constant cold-start latency)
2026-10-29 02:40:00 [INFO] nightly-reconciliation -> CONTAINER (exceeds Lambda 15-min limit; use ECS or Step Functions)
2026-10-29 02:40:00 [WARNING] Indexer cold start latency: 800 ms (new env init)
2026-10-29 02:40:00 [INFO] Indexer warm start latency: 15 ms (reused env)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Workload → WorkloadPlacement.place()
    │
    ├─ duration > 15 min? ──yes──→ CONTAINER / Step Functions
    │
    ├─ event-driven & bursty? ─yes─→ LAMBDA
    │        │
    │        ▼ invocation
    │   cold start? ─yes─→ init env (download code, start JVM) +800ms
    │                └no→ reuse warm env +15ms
    │   (stateless: persist state to DynamoDB/S3, not local disk)
    │
    └─ steady/always-on? ─────────→ CONTAINER (ECS/EKS)

  Memory ↑ → CPU ↑ (coupled). Payload/package/concurrency have hard limits.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I choose AWS Lambda over a container when the workload is genuinely event-driven, short-lived, and spiky or infrequent, because Lambda runs only when an event arrives, scales automatically from zero to thousands of concurrent executions, and bills per millisecond, so it costs nothing when idle. That is a perfect fit for reacting to an S3 upload, processing a queue message, or a lightweight API with bursty traffic. I keep the workload on a container in ECS or EKS when it is long-running, steady, latency-sensitive in a way cold starts would hurt, needs full runtime control, or simply exceeds Lambda's limits, because a steady process is cheaper and more predictable on a container.

The constraints I always weigh are four. Cold starts: when Lambda spins up a fresh execution environment it adds initialization latency from tens of milliseconds to a few seconds, which is worse for Java because the JVM takes time to start, so I initialize expensive clients once outside the handler and use provisioned concurrency or SnapStart for latency-sensitive paths. The fifteen-minute maximum execution time: anything longer must be a container or be broken into steps with Step Functions. Memory and CPU coupling: I set memory and CPU scales with it, so a CPU-bound function sometimes gets extra memory purely to buy CPU. And statelessness: each invocation may run in a different environment with no reliable local state, so any state goes to DynamoDB, S3, or a cache, and I treat the small `/tmp` space as ephemeral.

The senior nuance I add is that there are also limits on payload size, package size, and concurrency, and long synchronous chains of Lambdas can be both slow and costly, so Lambda is not a universal hammer.

At National Bank of India I ran the statement-PDF indexer as a Lambda because it fires a few hundred times a day in bursts and costs nothing between runs, and I initialized its clients outside the handler to blunt cold starts. I kept the transfer API on ECS Fargate because it serves steady traffic all day and I did not want to pay cold-start latency on every scale-out. And the nightly reconciliation job, which runs about forty minutes, could not be a single Lambda because of the fifteen-minute limit, so I ran it as an ECS task orchestrated by Step Functions. That mix is exactly how I apply the rule: Lambda for short, event-driven, bursty work, containers for long-running, steady, or heavy work.

---

keyPoints: Lambda: serverless compute — run code without servers
Event-driven: triggered by S3, API Gateway, SQS, DynamoDB
Pay per invocation — no charge when idle
Cold start: first invocation slower — keep warm for latency-sensitive
